questions.q: Why does a trade execute at the resting order's price, not the incoming (aggressor) order's price?
options: Using the aggressor's price would let an aggressively-priced order fill at a worse price than what was actually available on the book -- the resting price is what was genuinely offered
The aggressor's price is always used in real exchanges, not the resting price
This is an arbitrary implementation choice with no real consequence
It doesn't matter which price is used since they are always identical
questions.explain: The resting order already committed to its price; the trade honors that price rather than the incoming order's (potentially worse, for the resting side) limit price.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does the 60-share buy order fill against id 1 BEFORE id 2, even though both rest at the identical price of 100.10?
options: Both orders are filled simultaneously, with no real ordering between them
The order with the lower id number is always filled last
id 1 always has priority over id 2 regardless of arrival time
Price-time priority: at the same price, the order that arrived earlier (id 1) is matched first
questions.explain: This is price-time priority actually working: when prices tie, the earlier-arriving order is matched first -- exactly what id 1 (added before id 2) demonstrates.

questions.q: Why can a single incoming order match against MULTIPLE resting orders in sequence?
options: The matching loop keeps consuming resting liquidity, best price first, until the incoming order is fully filled or no longer crosses the book
This only happens when the incoming order's price exactly equals the resting price
Matching against multiple orders is a bug that should be prevented
An incoming order can only ever match against exactly one resting order
questions.explain: A large incoming order can "walk the book," consuming several price levels or several orders at one level, filling as much as possible before any remainder rests.

questions.q: Why does cancellation search by order ID instead of by price?
options: Searching by price alone would be ambiguous whenever multiple orders share the same price level -- ID uniquely identifies which specific order to remove
Cancellation by price would work correctly in all cases
Searching by price is actually faster and more reliable than searching by ID
Order IDs and prices are always identical in this simulator
questions.explain: Multiple orders can rest at the same price (as id 1 and id 2 both did at 100.10) -- only a unique ID unambiguously identifies which one to cancel.

questions.q: What happens to the unfilled remainder of an order that only partially matches against the book?
options: It becomes a new resting order on the book, at the back of the line for its price level -- it does not simply disappear
The order is filled anyway at a worse price to force completion
The entire order, including the already-matched portion, is reversed
The unfilled remainder is automatically cancelled
questions.explain: An order that isn't fully matched keeps its remaining quantity and rests on the book as a new order, maintaining the already-executed trades for the portion that did match.
